extracted.intended_audience: attorneys who practice before the USPTO (trademark/non-patent), respondents and counsel in USPTO reciprocal disciplinary proceedings, and OED/USPTO personnel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria the USPTO Director applies when deciding whether to impose reciprocal discipline based on a state's disciplinary adjudication under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24, including defenses a respondent must prove and procedural requirements for nunc pro tunc/concurrent discipline and reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director's presumption to impose identical reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall consider the record and shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner demonstrates by clear and convincing evidence, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact that one of the specified defenses applies (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The starting point is a federal-level presumption in favor of imposing the same discipline the state imposed; the Office will apply the identical sanction unless a respondent meets the strict, enumerated exceptions by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deprivation of due process (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: "The procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process requires reasonable notice of the charges and opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner (e.g., notice of charges before proceedings, ability to present evidence, testify, call and cross-examine witnesses, and make arguments). The inquiry is whether the other jurisdiction's procedure was so lacking as to constitute denial of due process — not whether USPTO procedures here were perfect. Precedents: Mathews v. Eldridge; In re Ruffalo; In re Squire; In re Zdravkovich.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: There was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must show by clear and convincing evidence that the proof of misconduct in the prior proceeding was so inadequate or flawed that the USPTO could not accept the state decision as final. This is a demanding, narrow standard; federal review is not a retrial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: The imposition of the same public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in a grave injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct (i.e., whether the sanction imposed by the state was so ill-fitted that imposing it federally would be unjust). Relevant considerations include whether the state sanction was within the appropriate range of penalties. Personal, financial, or client hardship alone is generally insufficient unless it demonstrates disproportionality; mitigating factors already considered by the state court cannot be relitigated to further reduce the sanction here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument that practitioner was not publicly disciplined (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior disposition was not a public discipline of the types listed, that may be a basis to resist reciprocal discipline. The Office examines whether the prior action qualifies as the type of public discipline that triggers reciprocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent's burden and standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The respondent must demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that there is a genuine issue of material fact as to one of the defenses enumerated in § 11.24(d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal and USPTO precedent treat this burden narrowly; courts and the Director will not act as a reviewing court to re-weigh evidence absent clear and convincing proof of a Selling-element deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline proceedings are not de novo
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal disciplinary proceedings are not in any sense de novo proceedings; the Director or federal tribunal is not retrying the original disciplinary case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collateral attacks on the underlying proceedings, factual re-litigation, or arguments that merely challenge the merits without meeting § 11.24(d) standards are improper. Federal review is limited to the narrow Selling factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service and notice under § 11.35 and effect of mail service
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice and order must be served in accordance with § 11.35, which permits service by mail or any delivery service that provides confirmation of delivery or attempted delivery to a respondent not registered at the last address known to the OED Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mail service without a signature may still be proper (e.g., posting on the door and/or attempted delivery can satisfy notice per Jones v. Flowers). Lack of a recipient's signature does not automatically establish deprivation of process; the key inquiry includes whether the respondent received notice and was prejudiced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudice requirement for service/notice challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevail on a service/notice challenge, respondent must show prejudice from any alleged defective service (e.g., that lack of proper service prevented meaningful participation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the respondent actually received the decision or had a realistic opportunity to respond (filed responses, participated in the proceedings), courts reject service-based claims where no prejudice is shown (see In re Burbank; In re Jaffee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice: proper types of arguments and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The grave injustice inquiry is limited to whether the sanction is disproportionate to the misconduct; arguments about collateral personal/professional hardship or that the discipline would burden clients are generally not pertinent unless they show disproportionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the prior sanction was outside the range of appropriate penalties for the misconduct or that some extraordinary circumstance makes imposing the same sanction a 'grave injustice.' Simply being a respected attorney, having no prior discipline, or having significant client burdens—particularly where the respondent agreed to the discipline—will not normally meet this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nunc pro tunc (concurrent) reciprocal discipline requirements (§ 11.24(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline may be imposed nunc pro tunc only if the practitioner promptly notified the OED Director of his or her disbarment/suspension in another jurisdiction, and establishes by clear and convincing evidence that the practitioner voluntarily ceased all activities related to practice before the Office and complied with all provisions of § 11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule is strictly enforced: mere cessation of practice is insufficient. The practitioner bears the burden to prove prompt notice and full compliance with § 11.58 by clear and convincing evidence. Precedents refuse nunc pro tunc treatment where notice to the OED was not given or § 11.58 obligations were not satisfied (e.g., In re Plache; In re Pioche).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of disciplined practitioners (§ 11.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disciplined practitioner must comply with duties enumerated in § 11.58, which include, among other things, filing notices of withdrawal in each patent and trademark matter pending before the USPTO and providing notice of the discipline to State and Federal jurisdictions and to all clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance with § 11.58 is required for reinstatement and for any nunc pro tunc/concurrent treatment; failure to satisfy these duties supports imposition of reciprocal discipline without concurrent credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement procedures (§ 11.58 & § 11.60) and non-automatic reinstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspended practitioner will not be automatically reinstated at the end of the suspension; a suspended or excluded practitioner shall not resume practice before the Office until reinstated and must comply with § 11.58 and petition for reinstatement under § 11.60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO reinstatement procedures differ from some state bars (which may have automatic reinstatement). Reciprocal discipline may therefore include requirements (e.g., petitioning for reinstatement) even if the original jurisdiction provides automatic reinstatement; the Office will make reciprocal discipline 'as close to identical as possible' given its rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline will be identical or as close as rules permit
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal discipline ordinarily will be identical—or as close to identical as local rules and circumstances permit—to the discipline imposed by the prior authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where exact identity is impossible (e.g., state rules provide automatic reinstatement but USPTO does not), the USPTO will impose the closest available equivalent (e.g., same suspension length but with a reinstatement petition requirement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors considered by the original tribunal are not relitigable to further reduce sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors already considered by the state court in fashioning the original discipline cannot be re-used in the reciprocal proceeding to obtain additional mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO will not revisit the state's weighing of mitigating circumstances; arguments that merely re-present the same mitigation considered by the state generally fail to show grave injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper scope of collateral challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Collateral attacks on the factual findings, credibility determinations, or negotiated nature of the state proceeding are not an appropriate vehicle to avoid reciprocal discipline under § 11.24.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that the state decision was motivated by resource conservation, negotiation artifacts, or lack of OED Director personal knowledge do not, by themselves, satisfy the Selling factors; the respondent must meet the statutory exceptions with clear and convincing evidence.
